questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: My desire to experience living in Italy, as I have always been very fond of the country and the culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, no real issues

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: None really

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *

How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was fairly easy. Sites such as HousingAnywhere and Spotahome have large selections of rooms available for rent.

I would recommend starting your housing-search a month or two in advance, as the demand exceedes the supply. Also, try and find a place not too far out of the centro storico, so that everything is still in walking distance.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: That it is the only option. There are no on-campus housing opportunities in Bologna. You'll likely live with other international students, Italian students or young Italian workers.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You need to update your study plan with the courses you want to follow, wait for it to get approved and register for the exams when they become available.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Whenever I was in doubt, I just asked other students.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had to change 3 of them, one because it wasn't taught in english, another because it was held in the next semester instead, and the third because I decided to attend a different class.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Notice the relevant information of the courses (teaching language, semester, etc.), look for the official course programmes when they are released, and remember to update your study plan with the courses you want to follow.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The main difference is that the semester is split into two parts, where the first part finishes in the beginning of November. This means that the end of the first part can get quite hectic with assignments, presentations and exams piling up. I would therefore recommend having a balance of courses over the entire semester.

Also, written exams are quite short, 1-1.5 hours with no teaching aids. Some people like this and some don't. I personally preferred that over the 3-5 hour open-book exams that we're used to in Denmark, but not everyone agrees. So, something to bear in mind.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It felt the same as in Denmark.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was pretty similar with maybe a little greater focus on active class participation.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. History of Economic Thought
2. Risk Management
3. Political Economy in Macroeconomics
4. International Monetary Economics
5. Machine Learning for Economists

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Well, Professor Bajo in Risk Management was a very good and engaging professor, and the book in History of Economic Thought was very interesting (although be wary if it is still held online only)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None really (maybe the high service fees for the housing websites, but not really unexpected, per se)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Milk and fruit were more expensive than anticipated! On the flip side, public transportation isn't really necessary as the city is very compact and walkable.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't really use the offers from the university.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not completely sure, but there's a gym (quite pricey though) and a swimming pool at least.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Take advantage of Bologna's central location to visit the rest of the country, hang out in the streets and bars in the evenings, and find some people to play sports with.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go and see San Luca (a monastery in the hills), wander the hills of Bologna, go on daytrips and weekendtrips to the rest of the country (especially places like Napoli, Rome, Torino, Verona, Cinque Terre and San Marino).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I'm used to being a little late and eating quite late, so the adjustment wasn't that big for me.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Learn a little italian, and when speaking english, talk a little slower and make them comfortable so that they are not so shy about speaking english themselves.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The language barrier was still the main issue. I was somewhat negatively surprised by how limited their english were/is (and my expectations weren't particularly high). It seems like no italians +35 speak a word of english, and the younger ones are mostly either too shy to speak it or are at a quite basic level.

However, it is not an issue, you can easily get by. Besides, there are a ton of international students.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food, the landscapes, the architecture, the history.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Start your housing-search a few months in advance and find a place not too far out of the centro storico
2. Learn a little italian (it makes it easier to shop and travel)
3. Attend events, socialize with your housemates and be yourself.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think I have covered most aspects.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Visiting and exploring all the beautiful cities and places that Italy has to offer, mingling with the locals and the international students.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Probably when the Danish and Italian authorities lowered the validity of the green pass/coronapas, which created some difficulties.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Bologna is not a big city, but it is very cozy, walkable and nice place to live. Also, it has great travel connections to the rest of country and it has a huge student population.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
